items.tx:
Politicians in Washington tried for decades to retire the A-10 Warthog attack jet, calling it too slow and outdated.

Then U.S. Air Force Captain Kim Campbell flew hers home from Baghdad with zero hydraulics, one damaged engine, and over one hundred and fifty shrapnel holes in the tail.

On April 7, 2003, American ground troops were pinned down under heavy fire in the middle of Baghdad. Twenty-seven-year-old Captain Campbell dove through thick clouds to deliver close air support with her thirty-millimeter cannon.

As she pulled up after saving the troops on the ground, an Iraqi surface-to-air missile exploded directly against the rear of her aircraft.

The blast severed both of her redundant hydraulic lines at the same time, punched a football-sized hole through the right tail stabilizer, and damaged her right jet engine. Instantly, the flight stick went dead. The nose of the aircraft rolled violently toward the streets of Baghdad below.

Why did she not pull the ejection handle?

Because ejecting over central Baghdad meant parachuting straight into the hands of hostile militia, and forcing dozens of American soldiers to risk their lives in an urban ambush just to rescue her.

Sitting inside the A-10's twelve-hundred-pound titanium armor tub, Campbell flipped a single emergency switch on her console called Manual Reversion.

That switch locked the flight stick directly to physical steel cables, pulleys, and cranks running through the wings. Flying an A-10 on steel cables is like steering a heavy dump truck with no power steering at three hundred miles per hour.

For one full hour across three hundred miles of hostile sky, Campbell hauled the heavy stick with both hands using sheer muscle power.

The hardest part was landing. Without hydraulics, she had no wing flaps to slow down, no speed brakes, and no nose-wheel steering. If she touched down and the tires blew, the jet would cartwheel in flames.

She brought the crippled Warthog down onto the runway at nearly two hundred miles per hour, fighting the rudder pedals with her legs until the battered aircraft rolled to a stop.

When her crew chief climbed the ladder and saw hundreds of holes in the aluminum skin, he could only shake his head in disbelief.

Never mock old American steel, and never bet against the pilot sitting inside it.

items.t: He left the most powerful office in the world humiliated. Two decades later, a President flew 1,000 miles just to prove he'd been right all along. January 20,…
items.tx:
He left the most powerful office in the world humiliated.

Two decades later, a President flew 1,000 miles just to prove he'd been right all along.

January 20, 1953. Harry Truman walked out of the White House at 68 years old with one of the lowest approval ratings in American history.

The newspapers had declared his presidency a failure.

Washington breathed a sigh of relief.

He returned to Independence, Missouri. To Bess. To their modest house on Delaware Street.

To a life without Secret Service, without staff, without the trappings of power.

Just an Army veteran with a pension and his dignity.

That spring, he did something no former president had ever done: he bought a Chrysler and drove himself—with only Bess beside him—across America.

No motorcade. No security.

Just two people stopping at gas stations, eating at diners, waving at stunned strangers who couldn't believe their eyes.

He answered his own telephone. He wrote thousands of letters by hand.

He walked the streets of his hometown every single morning, moving so fast that reporters struggled to keep up.

And while he lived quietly, history was working in his favor.

He had desegregated the Armed Forces when it could have ended his career.

He had stood against Soviet expansion at the exact moment the free world needed him to.

He had championed the Marshall Plan that rebuilt a shattered Europe.

And in 1945—twenty years before it would become reality—he stood before Congress and demanded something radical: national health insurance for every American.

They called it socialism.

They called him reckless.

They killed the bill without mercy.

He never apologized. He never retreated.

He simply waited.

Then came July 30, 1965.

President Lyndon Johnson could have signed Medicare into law in the Rose Garden.

Instead, he boarded Air Force One and flew to Independence, Missouri—to a small library in an old man's hometown.

When Johnson rose to speak, he turned to the 81-year-old man sitting beside him.

The man the world had written off.

The man who had been mocked, dismissed, forgotten.

And he said:

"The people of the United States love and voted for Harry Truman, not because he gave them hell—but because he gave them hope."

Then he signed the bill that would change millions of lives.

And handed Harry Truman the very first Medicare card ever issued in the United States of America.

Bess received the second.

The man who had left Washington in silence.

The man who had spent two decades being unpopular, then ignored, then undeniably right—sat in his own library, in his own town, and held proof that his vision had finally come to pass.

He died in 1972. Today, historians rank him among the greatest American presidents.

He didn't change his principles to earn that honor. He didn't soften his record or chase approval.

He remained exactly who he was—and trusted that the work would speak for itself, even when the world had stopped listening.

History doesn't move at the speed we need.

But it moves.

And sometimes—if you're principled enough, patient enough, and brave enough to be unpopular—it circles back and vindicates you.

Even if it takes twenty years, a thousand-mile flight, and a small card pressed into an old man's weathered hands.

Some people aren't ahead of their time.

They're just ahead of the recognition they deserve.

Why do you think stories like this disappear from history?

This is what happens when historical ignorance is accompanied by an astonishing degree of intellectual arrogance.

First, there were no “West African countries” during the transatlantic slave trade. The region comprised kingdoms, empires, city-states and independent societies. Applying modern national identities to centuries-old history is an extraordinary display of ignorance.

Second, Europeans did not arrive in Africa as benevolent abolitionists. For centuries, they financed, institutionalised and industrialised human trafficking, supplying weapons that fuelled wars and slave raids, creating an enormous market for human captives, and codifying racial slavery into their laws. African collaborators existed, but their complicity does not absolve the European empires that sustained this monstrous commerce.

Entire African communities were devastated, populations displaced, villages destroyed and societies destabilised. Millions were deported across the Atlantic, while countless others suffered captivity, violence and death on African soil. Africa was itself a vast crime scene, not merely the departure point of enslaved people.

And perhaps the most remarkable historical fraud is how European nations have managed to present themselves as the liberators of the very people they spent centuries enslaving.

I grew up in a former French colony in Africa being taught from primary school that slavery was abolished by a Frenchman named Victor Schœlcher. It was only in 2026 ( yes this year ) that I discovered that people in former British colonies had been taught a remarkably similar story, except that their white saviour was an Englishman named William Wilberforce.

Yet long before Britain abolished slavery in its colonies in 1833, enslaved Africans in Haiti had fought a revolution, defeated European armies and proclaimed their independence in 1804. Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines were central to that struggle.

In 1816, Haitian President Alexandre Pétion supplied Simón Bolívar with weapons, ammunition and military assistance to support South America’s liberation struggles, on the condition that he advance the emancipation of enslaved people. And he went on to free more than half a dozen Latin American countries. 

And what was Haiti’s reward for daring to liberate itself? Diplomatic isolation and, in 1825, a crushing indemnity of 150 million francs imposed by France, effectively forcing formerly enslaved people to compensate the descendants of their enslavers for the loss of their supposed property.

Meanwhile, Britain compensated slave owners with £20 million following abolition, while the enslaved received nothing.

Where are these stories in the European narratives of abolition? Where are Nat Turner, who led an enslaved uprising in Virginia in 1831, Queen Nzinga, who resisted Portuguese expansion and slave raiding in Central Africa, or the countless African rulers, communities and freedom fighters who resisted enslavement?

Black people fought for their freedom. They rebelled, resisted, organised, sacrificed and died for it. Their liberation was never simply a gift bestowed upon them by benevolent Europeans.

There is something profoundly tragic about descendants of enslaved Africans, born and educated in the lands of their ancestors’ enslavers, regurgitating sanitised colonial history, seemingly incapable of distinguishing historical scholarship from imperial propaganda.

The greatest triumph of colonial indoctrination is when the descendants of its victims become the most zealous defenders of its mythology.

Ok, final Texas thoughts. 

Summary: I am being a pessimist and think polls overestimate Trump-D persuasion, as well as blue non-voter lean. 

NYT Siena and Atlas Intel are objectively very good polls for the Dem side - but I still don't quite believe them. 

1) Atlas didn't directly publish recall but its persuasion splits in Sen/Gov makes sense. So how do we get D+6 Sen and D+2 Gov? They think Non-2024 voters are breaking 90% D. Insanity. 

2) NYT Siena has Trump +11 recall (the red end of what I think the final post-eday settles around), so that's fine. 

In Gov:
They have 2% of Harris voters voting for Abbott (reasonable). 7% of Trump voters voting for Hinojosa seems pretty high to me. 

In Sen:
They have 1% of Harris voters voting for Paxton (the remaining Dixiecrats?), while 9% of Trump voters vote Talarico. That seems pretty high, given what is going on. 

Additionally, NYT Siena has D+40 Sen and D+27 Gov for non-2024 voters. While I do think they will lean blue, my D+1 rests on a far more conservative D+20 and D+15 assumption in both races. 

The Trump Recall is correct, but my hypothesis is that the Republicans here are not as Trumpy as the ones that are expected to show up in the Deluge tomorrow. I can't prove persuasion but I am guessing the quickly elevating rural white turnout in days 10-12 of EV is carrying into E-Day as I suggested might happen. 

Remember 2022 - outside of MI/WI/PA/a few other states, it was a wave of red carnage against Dems. I am positing that TX will be a similar situation. Dems can win, but it will *not* be significantly amplified by turnout differentials like NC/GA/FL to an extent which everyone thought was safe until a few weeks ago.

A surge of Dark MAGA Republicans who vote red down the ballot might still find Ken Paxton a bridge too far, but all the other Democratic statewides would probably want lower turnout.
